senses.def: to heat a liquid until it bubbles and turns to steam, or to reach that temperature
examples: Wait until the water boils before you add the pasta.
She boiled the eggs for exactly seven minutes.

senses.def: to cook food in very hot, bubbling water
examples: Boil the potatoes until they are soft enough to mash.

note: "Boil down to" means "to be basically about": It all boils down to money. American English says "bring to a boil".

senses.def: confident and willing to take risks or say what you think
examples: The new mayor made a bold decision to ban cars from downtown.
It was a bold move to quit her job and start a company.

senses.def: very clear and strong in color or shape, so it is easy to notice; printed in thick letters
examples: The poster uses bold colors to catch people's attention.
Key terms are printed in bold.

senses.def: a weapon that explodes, either dropped from a plane or left somewhere
examples: Police evacuated the station after a bomb was found in a bag.
The bomb exploded just after midnight.

senses.def: to attack a place with bombs
examples: Enemy planes bombed the bridge to cut off supply routes.

senses.def: (informal) to fail badly, especially a movie, show, or test
examples: The movie bombed at the box office despite its huge budget.

note: The final b is silent: /bɑːm/. Informal "bomb" (fail) is American; in British English "go down a bomb" means succeed.

senses.def: an attack in which a bomb is exploded or dropped
examples: Dozens of people were injured in the bombing at the market.
No group has claimed responsibility for the bombing.

senses.def: a feeling or shared experience that connects people closely
examples: The two sisters share a strong bond.
Playing on the same team helped build a bond between the boys.

senses.def: a document promising that a government or company will pay back money it has borrowed, with interest
examples: Many retirees invest in government bonds because they are low-risk.

senses.def: to develop a close relationship with someone
examples: The new employees bonded over lunch during their first week.

senses.def: one of the hard parts that make up the skeleton of a person or animal
examples: He broke a bone in his wrist when he fell off his bike.
The dog buried a bone in the backyard.

note: Idioms: "have a bone to pick with someone" (want to complain to them), "bone dry" (completely dry).

senses.def: extra money added to someone's pay, usually as a reward for good work
examples: Every employee received a year-end bonus after a record year.
Her bonus depends on how many sales she makes.

senses.def: something good that you get in addition to what you expected
examples: The hotel is close to the beach, and free breakfast is a bonus.

senses.def: a set of printed pages fixed together inside a cover, or the same text in electronic form
examples: I read a great book about the history of New York.
She has written three books on climate change.

senses.def: to arrange in advance to have a seat, room, ticket, or appointment
examples: We booked a table for eight o'clock.
The flights were fully booked weeks ago.

note: "Do something by the book" means following the rules exactly. Americans also say "make a reservation" for book.

senses.def: an arrangement made in advance to reserve a room, seat, or ticket
examples: You can make a booking online or by phone.
The hotel canceled our booking without any warning.

note: More common in British English; Americans usually say "reservation". "Booking fee" is common in both.

senses.def: a sudden period of fast growth in business, sales, or popularity
examples: The city grew rapidly during the oil boom of the 1970s.
There has been a boom in online shopping.

senses.def: a loud, deep sound, like an explosion
examples: We heard a loud boom as the thunder rolled over the hills.

senses.def: to grow or become successful very quickly
examples: Business is booming now that tourists are coming back.

note: Opposite: bust or slump. "Baby boomers" are people born during the population boom after 1945.

senses.def: to increase something or help it become more successful
examples: The government cut taxes to boost the economy.
Winning the first game really boosted the team's confidence.

senses.def: something that helps or encourages someone or something
examples: The new factory will give a major boost to local employment.

note: A "booster" or "booster shot" is an extra dose of a vaccine.

senses.def: a strong shoe that covers the foot, ankle, and sometimes part of the leg
examples: You'll need waterproof boots for the hike.
She bought a pair of leather boots for the winter.

senses.def: to start a computer so it is ready to use
examples: My laptop takes forever to boot up in the morning.

note: In British English, the boot is a car's storage space; Americans call it the "trunk".

senses.def: the official line that separates two countries or regions
examples: We crossed the border into Canada early in the morning.
The town is right on the border with Mexico.

senses.def: a strip around the edge of something, often for decoration
examples: The invitation had a thin gold border.

senses.def: to share a border with another country or area
examples: Turkey borders eight countries, including Greece and Georgia.

note: "Border on" also means "come close to": His behavior bordered on rude.

senses.def: feeling tired and impatient because something is not interesting or you have nothing to do
examples: The kids got bored after an hour in the car.
I'm bored with doing the same thing every day.

note: Common trap: "I am bored" (I feel it) vs. "I am boring" (I make others feel it).

senses.def: not interesting, making you feel tired and impatient
examples: The lecture was so boring that half the class fell asleep.
Filling out tax forms is boring but necessary.

note: The thing is boring; the person is bored. Don't say "I am boring" when you mean "I am bored".

senses.def: used in "be born" to talk about the beginning of someone's life
examples: I was born in Izmir in 1995.
Their first child was born last spring.

senses.def: having a natural ability for something
examples: She's a born teacher who can explain anything clearly.

note: Always passive: "I was born", never "I born". Do not confuse with "borne" (past participle of bear).

senses.def: to take and use something that belongs to someone else, planning to give it back
examples: Can I borrow your charger for a minute?
They borrowed money from the bank to buy a house.

senses.def: to take an idea, word, or method from somewhere else and use it
examples: English has borrowed many words from French.

note: Borrow = take from someone; lend = give to someone. Say "Can I borrow your pen?", not "Can you borrow me...".

senses.def: the person in charge of you at work
examples: I need to ask my boss if I can leave early on Friday.
She's been her own boss since she opened the bakery.

senses.def: to tell people what to do in an annoying way
examples: Stop bossing your little brother around!

senses.def: used to talk about two people or things together
examples: Both my parents are teachers.
You can park on both sides of the street.

senses.def: the two people or things, considered together
examples: I couldn't decide between the shirts, so I bought both.
Both of them arrived late.

note: "Both X and Y" is the pattern: Both Ali and Can passed. For negatives, use "neither": Neither of them came.

senses.def: to make the effort to do something, usually in negative sentences
examples: He didn't even bother to say goodbye.
Don't bother cooking tonight; we'll order pizza.

senses.def: to annoy, worry, or interrupt someone
examples: Sorry to bother you, but do you know where the station is?
It really bothers me when people talk during movies.

senses.def: a glass or plastic container with a narrow neck, used for liquids
examples: Always carry a bottle of water when you go running.
They opened a bottle of wine to celebrate.

senses.def: to put a liquid into bottles
examples: The juice is bottled at a factory near the orchards.

note: "Bottle up" your feelings means hiding them instead of expressing them.

senses.def: the lowest part or surface of something
examples: The keys were at the bottom of my bag.
Sign your name at the bottom of the page.

senses.def: in the lowest or last position
examples: The plates are on the bottom shelf.
Our team finished in the bottom three this season.

collocations: from the bottom of my heart
note: "The bottom line" is the most important fact. "Get to the bottom of" means find the real cause.

senses.def: to move quickly away from a surface after hitting it, or to make something do this
examples: The ball bounced off the wall and hit the window.
Kids love bouncing on the trampoline.

senses.def: to be returned because there is not enough money in the account or the address is wrong
examples: My email bounced because I typed the address wrong.

note: "Bounce back" means recover quickly after a problem: The economy bounced back.

senses.def: certain or very likely to happen (bound to do something)
examples: With so many guests, something is bound to go wrong.
You're bound to feel nervous on your first day.

senses.def: forced by law, duty, or a promise to do something
examples: The company is legally bound to protect your data.

senses.def: traveling toward a particular place
examples: The train was bound for Chicago when it broke down.

note: Also the past form of "bind". "Out of bounds" means a place you are not allowed to go.

senses.def: a line that marks the edge of an area and separates it from another
examples: The river forms the boundary between the two counties.
A fence marks the boundary of our property.

senses.def: the limit of what is acceptable or of what is known
examples: It's healthy to set clear boundaries with your coworkers.
Scientists keep pushing the boundaries of medicine.

note: "Border" is mainly for countries; "boundary" is for any edge or limit, including personal and abstract ones.

senses.def: to bend your head or body forward to show respect or to say thank you
examples: The actors bowed as the audience stood and clapped.
He bowed his head in prayer.

senses.def: the act of bending your head or body forward as a sign of respect
examples: The pianist took a bow at the end of the concert.

senses.def: to finally agree to do what others want (bow to)
examples: The company bowed to public pressure and withdrew the ad.

note: Pronounced /baʊ/ (like "now") for bending. "Bow" /boʊ/ is a different word: a ribbon knot or a weapon for arrows.

senses.def: a deep round dish used for food or liquid
examples: I had a bowl of soup for lunch.
Mix the flour and eggs in a large bowl.

senses.def: (American) a big college football game played after the regular season
examples: Millions of people watch the Super Bowl every year.

note: "Bowl" as a verb is used in bowling and cricket.

senses.def: a container with flat sides and a base, often with a lid
examples: We packed all our books into cardboard boxes for the move.
She gave me a box of chocolates.

senses.def: a small square on a form where you write or put a mark
examples: Check the box if you agree to the terms.

note: "Think outside the box" means think creatively. "Box" as a verb also means to fight in boxing.

senses.def: a male child or young man
examples: A little boy was flying a kite in the park.
They have two boys and a girl.

senses.def: (informal, American) used to express surprise or strong feeling
examples: Boy, was I glad to get home after that trip!

senses.def: a man or boy that someone is having a romantic relationship with
examples: She's bringing her boyfriend to dinner on Sunday.
Her ex-boyfriend still texts her sometimes.

note: Means a romantic partner. For a male friend, say "a friend" or "a guy friend".

senses.def: the organ inside your head that controls thinking, feeling, and movement
examples: Sleep is essential for a healthy brain.
The accident caused minor brain damage.

senses.def: intelligence, or a very intelligent person who plans something
examples: She has the brains to become a great scientist.
He was the brains behind the whole project.

note: "Pick someone's brain" means ask an expert for advice. "Rack your brain" means think very hard.

senses.def: a part of a tree that grows out from the trunk
examples: A bird built its nest on a high branch.
The storm brought down several large branches.

senses.def: a local office or store that belongs to a larger organization
examples: The bank is closing several of its rural branches.

senses.def: a part or division of a subject, family, or government
examples: Neurology is a branch of medicine.

note: "Branch out" means start doing something new: The company branched out into clothing.

senses.def: a product or group of products made by a company under a particular name
examples: Which brand of coffee do you usually buy?
The company spent millions building its brand.

senses.def: to give a product a particular name, image, or identity
examples: The phones are branded with the store's own logo.

senses.def: to describe someone unfairly as a bad type of person
examples: He was branded a traitor for criticizing the government.

note: "Brand-new" means completely new. Use "brand" for products like food or clothes; for cars and machines, "make" is also common.

senses.def: willing to do things that are dangerous, painful, or difficult
examples: The brave firefighter ran back into the burning house.
It was brave of you to admit your mistake.

senses.def: to deal with an unpleasant situation in order to do something
examples: Thousands of fans braved the cold to watch the parade.

note: "Put on a brave face" means pretend to be fine when you are upset.

senses.def: an action that breaks a law, rule, or agreement
examples: Selling customer data was a clear breach of contract.
The minister resigned over a breach of security rules.

senses.def: a break in a wall or system that allows something to get through
examples: The data breach exposed the passwords of millions of users.

senses.def: to break a law, rule, or agreement
examples: The supplier breached the agreement by delivering late.

note: Formal and legal. Don't confuse with "breech" (the back part of a gun, or a baby born feet first).

senses.def: a basic food made from flour, water, and usually yeast, then baked
examples: I bought a loaf of fresh bread from the bakery.
Would you like some bread with your soup?

note: Uncountable: "some bread" or "a loaf / slice of bread", not "a bread". The "breadwinner" earns the family's money.

senses.def: to separate into pieces or stop working because of force, or to make this happen
examples: Be careful not to break those glasses.
The screen will break if you drop the phone on concrete.

senses.def: to fail to obey a rule or law, or to not keep a promise
examples: He was fined for breaking the speed limit.
Never break a promise to a child.

senses.def: a short time when you stop working or studying to rest
examples: Let's take a ten-minute break and then continue.
Students get a two-week break in the spring.

note: Irregular verb: break – broke – broken. "Give me a break!" (informal) means "Stop it, that's ridiculous".

senses.def: a time when a vehicle or machine stops working
examples: We had a breakdown on the highway and waited two hours for a tow truck.

senses.def: the failure of a relationship, system, or discussion
examples: The breakdown of the peace talks led to more fighting.
She went through a nervous breakdown after years of stress.

senses.def: a detailed list that divides something into its parts
examples: Can you send me a breakdown of the costs?

note: The noun is one word (breakdown); the verb is two (break down): The car broke down.

senses.def: the first meal of the day, eaten in the morning
examples: I usually have eggs and toast for breakfast.
The hotel serves breakfast until ten.

note: No article in general use: "have breakfast", not "have a breakfast" (unless described: "a big breakfast"). Pronounced /ˈbrekfəst/.

senses.tr: atılım, çığır açan gelişme, büyük ilerleme
senses.def: an important discovery or development that helps solve a problem
examples: Researchers made a major breakthrough in cancer treatment.
After weeks of talks, negotiators finally achieved a breakthrough.

senses.def: either of the two soft parts on a woman's chest that can produce milk
examples: Doctors recommend regular checks for breast cancer.
The baby fell asleep at her mother's breast.

senses.def: meat from the front part of a chicken or other bird
examples: Grill the chicken breasts for about six minutes per side.

note: For the general front of the body, use "chest". Pronounced /brest/, not like "beast".

senses.def: the air you take into your lungs and let out again
examples: Take a deep breath and try to relax.
I was out of breath after running up the stairs.

note: Breath /breθ/ is the noun; breathe /briːð/ is the verb. "Don't hold your breath" means "don't expect it to happen soon".

senses.def: to take air into your lungs and send it out again
examples: Breathe in slowly through your nose.
The smoke was so thick that we could hardly breathe.

note: Verb with -e: breathe /briːð/. "Breathe new life into" means make something active or successful again.

senses.def: the process of taking air into the lungs and letting it out
examples: Her breathing became slow and steady as she fell asleep.
Breathing exercises can help reduce anxiety.

note: "Breathing room/space" also means extra time or freedom: The loan gave us some breathing room.

senses.def: a particular type of animal, especially a dog, cat, or farm animal, developed by people
examples: Labradors are one of the most popular dog breeds in America.

senses.def: to produce young animals, or to keep animals in order to produce young
examples: Salmon swim upstream to breed.
The farm breeds horses for racing.

senses.def: to cause a feeling or situation to develop
examples: Poverty often breeds crime and frustration.

note: Irregular verb: breed – bred – bred. "Familiarity breeds contempt" is a common saying.

senses.def: a small block of baked clay used for building walls and houses
examples: They live in an old brick house near the river.
Workers laid the bricks one by one.

note: "Hit a brick wall" means reach a point where you cannot make progress.

senses.def: a woman who is getting married or has just gotten married
examples: The bride wore her grandmother's lace dress.
Everyone stood up as the bride walked down the aisle.

note: The man is the "groom" (or bridegroom). In Turkish "gelin" also means daughter-in-law, but English "bride" does not.

senses.def: a structure built over a river, road, or railroad so people can cross it
examples: The new bridge cut travel time across the river in half.
They walked across the Brooklyn Bridge at sunset.

senses.def: to reduce the difference or distance between two groups or things
examples: The program aims to bridge the gap between rich and poor students.

note: "Burn your bridges" means destroy a relationship so you can't go back. "We'll cross that bridge when we come to it" = deal with it later.

senses.def: lasting only a short time
examples: After a brief pause, the speaker continued.
We made a brief stop in Denver on the way.

senses.def: using few words
examples: Please keep your answers brief and to the point.

senses.def: to give someone the information they need about a situation
examples: The general briefed reporters on the latest developments.

note: "In brief" means "in a few words". A "briefing" is a meeting where people receive information.

senses.def: for a short time
examples: The power went out briefly during the storm.
She worked briefly as a waitress before college.

senses.def: in a few words
examples: Let me briefly explain how the system works.
